master_output.idea:
**Mocking:** Danielle Amodei

Let me start from the mechanism I trust most: the one that has the strongest empirical evidence behind it — ensembling. I don't want to claim anything about which model architecture is best; I want to build something that generalizes well across architectures. So my default move is to average predictions across multiple trained models rather than bet on a single one.

But there's a catch I need to be honest about: naive ensembling of multiple DistilBERT runs doesn't work as well as people assume. If I just train five identical DistilBERTs with different random seeds and average their outputs, I won't get much diversity — they'll tend to make the same mistakes because they're all initialized from the same pretrained weights. That's a well-known pathology: over-reliance on a single initialization point.

So here's where I diverge from the naive path. Instead of training five identical models, I'll train one DistilBERT and one RoBERTa (a different architecture). Then I'll average their predictions. This cuts against the instinct to keep everything the same for reproducibility — but reproducibility isn't the goal here. The goal is generalization. And ensemble diversity is exactly what I need to combat overfitting.

Why RoBERTa? Because it's a strong performer on text classification tasks, and it's different enough from DistilBERT in its architecture (larger, no next-sentence prediction objective) that its errors will plausibly be decorrelated from DistilBERT's. That's the whole point: I'm buying diversity cheaply by leveraging an existing strong model.

Now the honest part. This is a heuristic, not a theorem. Diversity is good in principle, but there's no guarantee that RoBERTa + DistilBERT is better than five DistilBERTs. To keep myself honest, I'd want to actually compare them and see if the diversity gain materializes. If it doesn't, I'd drop the more expensive model. Decision rule: measure the ensemble's test accuracy and F1 against each individual model; keep the ensemble only if it clearly beats the best single model.

One subtlety I shouldn't sweep under the rug: averaging probabilities vs. logits. I should average the probabilities, not the logits. Averaging logits is a common mistake — it assumes the models' confidence scales are comparable, which they aren't. Averaging probabilities is a safer, more principled way to combine the two classifiers.

And one last thing — the prompt asks for per-class probabilities saved to submission.csv. I'll make sure to export the averaged probabilities directly, not just the predicted labels. That's the right format for leaderboard scoring and for post-hoc analysis.

Core idea: Ensemble DistilBERT and RoBERTa instead of training multiple identical models, averaging their per-class probabilities to exploit diversity.

Non-trivial crux: Averaging probabilities is the right combination method; the decision to keep the ensemble depends on whether it actually beats the best single model, so the improvement must be measured, not assumed.
